newsitem.title: UK: Watchdog report on LME balanced, market users say.
newsitem.headline: Watchdog report on LME balanced, market users say.

text.p: Metals market dealers and analysts gave passing to high marks to a review of the London Metal Exchange (LME) by Britain's top financial watchdog, saying it targeted nagging concerns without calling for over-regulation.
The Securities and Investment Board on Thursday issued a wide-ranging report, sparked by the Sumitomo copper scandal, calling on the LME to provide more information and regulation.

"I think they did a pretty good job...if you over-regulate you scare people away but if you don't regulate enough you lose their confidence," said Wolfgang Becker, managing director of Iceni Commodities Brokerage in Hamburg.
"I think it basically reflects what the customers of the LME think," he added.
He welcomed the SIB call for the LME to provide more information, especially in inter-office trading.
"It would make the market more readable if you could see on your screen which trades have taken place and the volumes behind them," Becker said.
The LME's chief excutive, David King, said the LME welcomed the results of the review and intended to implement many of the changes once the issues had a public airing.

A senior metals market analyst said the review reflected many of the concerns frequently discussed in the marketplace, such as improving reporting on large positions and the way trades are cleared. But the recommendations, if implemented would not disrupt the routine functions of trading on the LME.
"The SIB recognised that the system ain't broke, it just needs an overhaul every once in a while," said the London-based analyst, who asked not to be named.

"At the end of the day, it doesn't matter how well regulated a market is. If an individual intends to commit a criminal act, and a company's internal system is lax, he'll do it. But the SIB recommendations will help make it less likely," he added.

The recommendations are likely to ruffle some feathers, particularly those regarding a revamping of the governance of the LME, one senior figure in the metals market said. The LME board is currently made up of 16 members, half of which are representatives of ring dealing members.
"From what I gather it looks like they have suggested reasonable changes and created a good opportunity for the board to update itself," he said.
"But there will be ring members who are going to be infuriated," he added.
Becker strongly agreed that the LME board needed reorganisation.
"I think this is a totally unfair system and gives the LME member firms a huge advantage," he said. "Managing directors of LME companies should not be on the board."
Iceni, which is not a member of the LME, said on Monday it was closing down the Hamburg office at the end of the year.
Becker said it was closing because the metals markets were based on trust, but that had deteriorated.
